documentNotes.title: General note
documentNotes.statement:
**General note.** Maybe not all problems have correct questions. Some questions (maybe the main question of the problem, maybe one of the subquestions) may make no real sense. In this case you have to write in your answer (in English or Russian): «**impossible situation – ситуация невозможна**». Of course, this answer has to be explained numerically or logically.

Data from the tables (Planetary data, stars, constants, etc.) may be used for solving every problem.

The answers «Да-Yes» or «Нет-No» has to be written in English or Russian.

problems.title: Solar radiation
problems.statement: Find, with how many percents the mass of the Sun is diminishing per year due to its radiation.

solution.statement:
**Theoretical round. Sketches for solutions. For preliminary work of Jury ONLY.**

**Note for jury and team leaders.** The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: Annual fractional mass loss
sections.statement:
$$E=4\pi R^2\cdot A\cdot\tau,\qquad E=mc^2,\qquad X=(m/M)\cdot100\%.$$

$R$ — Earth–Sun distance, $R=149600000000\,\mathrm m$.

$A$ — Solar constant, $A=1367\,\mathrm{W/m^2}$.

$\tau=1\text{ year}=3.16\cdot10^7\,\mathrm s$.

$c$ — speed of light, $c=299800000\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

$M$ — mass of the Sun, $M=1.989\cdot10^{-30}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

$$X=(4\pi R^2\cdot A\cdot\tau/c^2/M)\cdot100\%.$$

$$X=(4\pi A\tau(R/c)^2/M)\cdot100\%.$$

$$X=(0.068\cdot10^{-12})\cdot100\%=6.8\cdot10^{-12}\%.$$

*Transcription note: the source prints $10^{-30}$ in the solar mass, whereas its included question-data table gives $1989000\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$. The source's exponent and final answer are retained as printed.*

problems.title: Planetarium
problems.statement: Classical devices "planetaria" are arranged so that each group of stars is projected on a dome by a small optical system. Consider the planetarium of observatory “Bobek” which diameter of the hall (dome) is $2R = 10\ \mathrm{m}$. On slides of the constellations projected on the dome images of $0^{\mathrm{m}}$ stars have the size $l_0 = 0.1\ \mathrm{mm}$ (foils with hole-stars of the mentioned size are often used as these "slides").

parts.statement: Estimate what the parameters should be (decide yourself, which parameters are important here) of the objective of this optical system, so that the visitors sitting in the centre of the hall of the planetarium would perceive the "stars" as points (not as circles or nebulae).

Let's suppose that all slides have been removed for replacement by more perfect ones, and all the light began to be projected on the dome. What would the total stellar magnitude of the illuminated dome be (the artificial gray sky)? Would it be possible to read a newspaper in such an illuminance?

answer.value: −20.25 mag; yes, a newspaper can be read.

problems.statementAfterParts: The answers has to include a list of the necessary parameters with formulae and numerical values.

solution.statement:
**Theoretical round. Sketches for solutions. For preliminary work of Jury ONLY.**

**Note for jury and team leaders.** The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.statement:
The visible angular size of the “stars” should be less than the resolution of an eye, that is the linear size (diameter) of images of these “stars” on the dome would not exceed $L_0=\alpha\cdot R$, where $\alpha$ is the resolving power of a human eye in the dark (nearby $50''\approx2.5\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{rad}$), $R$ is the radius of the hall of the planetarium. In our case $L_0=\alpha\cdot R\approx2.5\cdot10^{-4}\cdot5\,\mathrm m\approx1.25\,\mathrm{mm}$.

The size of the image of one star appearing on the dome with the optical system is defined by two parameters:

a) The first parameter is geometrical, it is defined by the optical increase of the size of a star at its display on the dome. If the size of a star on a slide is $l_0=0.1\,\mathrm{mm}$, the size of the image is calculated by the formula of increase of the objective (lens): $L=\Gamma\cdot l_0=l_0\cdot R/r$, where $r$ is the distance from the mentioned hole in a foil to the projecting lens. According to the formula for a lens $1/R+1/r=1/F$. In our case the increasing factor should not exceed $\Gamma_0=L_0/l_0$, whence we find that the focal length of the system should be not less than

$$F=\frac{R}{\Gamma_0+1}=\frac{R}{L_0/l_0+1}\approx\frac{R l_0}{L_0}=\frac{R l_0}{\alpha R}=\frac{l_0}{\alpha}=\frac{0.1\,\mathrm{mm}}{2.5\cdot10^{-4}}\approx40\,\mathrm{cm}.$$

It is the first condition. The condition is quite feasible.

b) The second parameter is diffraction. It is defined by the size of the Airy disc, the angular size of a divergence of the rays from a dot source (the source being near to focus of a lens) is equal to $\lambda/D$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength (of order 500 nm or $5\cdot10^{-7}\,\mathrm m$), and $D$ is the diameter of the lens of the projecting optical system. Thus the size of the image of a dot source on the dome of radius $R$ is $R\cdot\lambda/D$. So we need a condition

$$R\lambda/D\le\alpha R,\qquad D\ge\lambda/\alpha\approx\frac{5\cdot10^{-7}\,\mathrm m}{2.5\cdot10^{-4}}\approx2\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm m=2\,\mathrm{mm}.$$

So, the second condition: the diameter of the objective should be not less than 2 mm. The condition is quite feasible as well.

By the way, we may notice that this value is easy to point out at once: it is the diameter of a pupil exposure that corresponds to the resolution of a human eye in the conditions of day light.

Formal answer: two parameters:

1. Focal length of the system $F\ge l_0/\alpha\approx40\,\mathrm{cm}$.

*Source gap: the continuation of the formal list is missing at the top of the next scanned page. The second condition, $D\ge2\,\mathrm{mm}$, is present in the preceding paragraph.*

*Source gap: the top of the scanned page is cut off. The surviving calculation begins with the following displayed formula; the missing opening is not reconstructed.*

$$L=\Gamma\cdot l_0,$$

where $\Gamma$ is the magnification coefficient of the projecting system, $\Gamma=R/r$, $r$ is the distance from the hole in the foil to the projecting lens. By the lens formula, $1/R+1/r=1/F$, but since $R\ll F$, one may use $\Gamma\approx R/F$.

$$L=\Gamma\cdot l_0\approx(R/F)\cdot l_0=12.5\cdot0.1\,\mathrm{mm}=1.25\,\mathrm{mm},$$

Accordingly, the area of the illuminated surface of the dome which gives the star $0^{\mathrm m}$ is equal to

$$S_{m0}=\pi L^2/4\approx1.23\,\mathrm{mm}^2.$$

After slides-foils have been removed the whole dome will be illuminated, i.e. a hemisphere of radius $R=5\,\mathrm m$ will shine, the area of shining surface is

$$S=2\pi R^2\approx157\,\mathrm m^2.$$

Thus, the shining area will be

$$K=S/S_{m0}=\frac{2\pi R^2}{\pi L^2/4}=8(R/L)^2=8(F/l_0)^2\approx130000000.$$

In terms of stellar magnitudes the difference is

$$\Delta m=2.5^{\mathrm m}\lg K=2.5^{\mathrm m}\lg(8(F/l_0)^2)\approx20.25^{\mathrm m}.$$

Thus, the stellar magnitude of the dome will be $0^{\mathrm m}-20.25^{\mathrm m}=-20.25^{\mathrm m}$. It gives an illuminance 400 times less, than the illuminance outdoors at clear sunny day, and in 1000 times larger than illuminance from full Moon. It corresponds approximately to indoors illuminance at daytime. Of course, it is possible to read without any problem.

We should note that the solution does not require the values of limiting stellar magnitude $6^{\mathrm m}$, the number of projecting systems for the hemisphere and the diameter of the dome of the planetarium.

*Transcription note: the source's inequality $R\ll F$ is retained, although its numerical approximation uses the opposite scale relation.*

solution.incompleteReason: The top of the source scan is cut off; missing opening/continuation lines are marked. All surviving supplied calculation is transcribed.

problems.title: Sunrise on Mars
problems.statement: The Polar Bear (whom was already met in the texts of many International Astronomy Olympiads) was tired to make astronomical observations on Earth. He made a fascinating journey to the North Pole of Mars, and decided to observe a sunrise there. Calculate how long this sunrise lasts. The solution has to include a picture with an image of the Bear on the North Pole of Mars. Necessary sizes or angular sizes should be in the picture. Assume that Mars is spherical and its orbit may be considered circular. Recollect for yourself the necessary information about the Polar Bear.

solution.statement:
**Theoretical round. Sketches for solutions. For preliminary work of Jury ONLY.**

**Note for jury and team leaders.** The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: Sunrise duration
sections.statement:
For an observer on the North Pole of Mars the sunrise happens once a year, in time close to the day of the martian vernal equinox. The solution of the problem is analogous to the solution about the sunrise on the Earth's poles, but we have to remember that some parameters are different on Mars and on Earth:

- $\alpha$ — the visible angular size of Sun.
- $v$ — the speed of the Sun along the planet's ecliptic.
- $\varepsilon$ — the inclination of the planet's equator plane to the plane of the planet's ecliptic.
- $R$ — radius of the planet.

For the observer on the North Pole of Mars the angle between the ecliptic and the horizon is equal to $\varepsilon=25.2^\circ$. During the sunrise the Sun goes up to the angle equal to its apparent angular diameter, that is

$$\alpha=D/L,$$

where $D$ is the diameter of the Sun, $L$ is the distance from Mars to the Sun. During this time the Sun moves an angular distance $\varphi=\alpha/\sin\varepsilon$ on the ecliptic. Thus, the duration of the sunset equals to $\tau=\varphi/v=\alpha/(v\sin\varepsilon)$, where $v$ is the speed of the Sun along the martial ecliptic.

Due to the large eccentricity of orbit of Mars both the distance $L$ and speed $v$ may vary significantly ($\pm e=9.3\%$ of mean value). Nevertheless we do not know a priory, and cannot understand from the tables, in which point of orbit Mars is situated at the moments of its vernal equinox. So we shall use mean values, equal to $L=228$ million km and $v=360^\circ/687^{\mathrm d}\approx0.524^\circ$ per day. Thus,

$$\tau=\frac{(1.392/228)\,\mathrm{rad}\times(180/\pi)\,{}^\circ/\mathrm{rad}}{(360^\circ/687^{\mathrm d})\sin25.2^\circ}\approx1.57\text{ days or }37.6\text{ hours}.$$

*Source note: “sunset” and the discussion of eccentricity are printed in this sunrise sketch; the question explicitly permits a circular orbit. The requested drawing of the Bear on Mars is not supplied in the available sketch.*

solution.incompleteReason: The supplied numerical sketch gives 37.6 hours but does not include the drawing of the Bear requested in the question.

problems.title: Photo of Jupiter
problems.statement:
In the photo of Jupiter that was taken on October 19, 2009, one of the Galilean moons and its shadow on the disc of the planet can be seen. Jupiter was near the middle of Capricornus constellation when the photo was taken.

Find the orbital distance from the moon to the surface of the planet. Determine the name of the moon. The solution should be illustrated by drawings. The name of the moon in the solution and in the drawings should be written (or duplicated) in English.

figures.alt: Colour photograph of Jupiter with a bright moon to the left and a dark circular moon shadow on its disc.
figures.caption: 4. Photo of Jupiter.

solution.statement:
**Theoretical round. Sketches for solutions. For preliminary work of Jury ONLY.**

**Note for jury and team leaders.** The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: Photo geometry and identification
sections.statement:
*Source gap: the opening of this solution is missing at the top edge of scanned page 4. The visible text starts mid-sentence:*

… moon (to the left) and to the shadow of the moon (to the right) the distance $L$ from the center of the moon to the center of Jupiter can be calculated using formulas of rectangular triangle:

$$L^2=[(a+b)/\tan\alpha+R]^2+a^2,$$

$$L/R=\left\{\left[\frac{a+b}{R\tan\alpha}+1\right]^2+(a/R)^2\right\}^{1/2}.$$

Where $\alpha$ is the angle between the direction to the Sun (The Sun beams come a little from the left) and the direction to the Earth (from where the picture is made). We can estimate this angle in two ways.

Or we remember that the Capricorn is a zodiac constellation, and the center of this constellation (not zodiac sign, but zodiac constellation!) is passed by the Sun approximately in the end of January — the beginning of February. The angle between the Sun positions on October, 19th and, assume, on February, 3rd, is equal 3.6 months or $108^\circ$.

Or to start with that fact that the picture is made on October, 19th (a direct ascension of the Sun 26 days after an equinox we will estimate as $12^{\mathrm h}+26\cdot4^{\mathrm m}=13^{\mathrm h}44^{\mathrm m}$), Jupiter was in the middle of Capricorn constellation (not zodiac sign, but constellation!) (right ascension of this point we will estimate to $21^{\mathrm h}$), and both the Sun and Jupiter were close to the ecliptic, declination of both points nearby $-10^\circ$–$-15^\circ$. This data allow us to estimate the angle between Sun and Jupiter at the celestial sphere as about the difference in declinations, that is, $7^{\mathrm h}16^{\mathrm m}$ or $109^\circ$.

From the second drawing, knowing this angle $\varphi$, and distances to the Sun from Earth $L_E$ and from Jupiter $L_J$, it is possible to calculate the angle corner $\alpha$ necessary to us:

$$L_J\sin\alpha=L_E\sin\varphi,\qquad\sin\alpha=(L_E/L_J)\sin\varphi.$$

$$\sin\alpha\approx(1/5.2)\sin108^\circ\approx(1/5.2)\cdot0.95\approx0.183.$$

$$\alpha\approx10.5^\circ.$$

By measuring the values **R, a and b** (accordingly 48.5 mm, 59 mm and 18 mm on the author printed picture, on other scaled printed pictures other values may be obtained, but their absolute values are not important, important is only ratios that do not depend on scale) in the photo, and using the formula for a rectangular triangle, we can receive a value of $L/R$ equal to 9.64.

From the given tables it is possible to find that for Io this ratio equals to 5.90, for Europa — 9.39, for Ganimede — 14.97, for Callisto — 26.33. It is evident, that our calculations are made with some accuracy, and the proximity of values 9.64 and 9.39 (1.5% of accuracy) says that we see the moon **Europa** in the picture.

*Transcription note: “difference in declinations” and “1.5%” follow the supplied sketch. The sketch reports distance from Jupiter's centre, while the question asks distance from its surface; a final subtraction of the radius is not explicitly supplied. The ray-diagram label at the bottom of scanned page 3 is partly cut off.*

problems.title: Jupiter disappeared
problems.statement: Let us suppose that Jupiter suddenly disappeared. The moons of Jupiter became independent bodies.

parts.statement: Which former Galileo moon(s) and in what case may leave the Solar system?

answer.value: Io, Europa, Ganimede and Callisto, in the escape sectors described in the sketch; the referenced sector diagram is absent.

parts.statement: Which former Galileo moon(s) and in what case may fall into the Sun?

answer.value: Io and Europa, at the two configurations near local conjunction described in the sketch; the referenced point diagram is absent.

problems.statementAfterParts: The answers “which moon” and “in what case” (configurations at the moment of Jupiter disappearance) have to be given in the form of drawings, and calculations should be the base for the answers. The names of the moons in the solution and in the drawings should be written in English. Consider the orbit of Jupiter (before its disappearance) to be circular.

solution.statement:
**Theoretical round. Sketches for solutions. For preliminary work of Jury ONLY.**

**Note for jury and team leaders.** The proposed sketches are not full; the team leaders have to give more detailed explanations for students. But the correct solutions in the students’ papers (enough for 8 pts) may be shorter.

sections.title: Orbital velocities
sections.statement:
Let us find the most important parameters that we need for the solution. The orbital velocities of Jupiter and its moons are,

Jupiter: $T=2\pi\cdot778600000/4332.59/86400=13.069\,\mathrm{km/s}$,

and analogously:

| Moon | Orbital velocity |
|---|---:|
| Io | 17.33 km/s |
| Europa | 13.74 km/s |
| Ganimede | 10.88 km/s |
| Callisto | 8.20 km/s |

After disappearance of Jupiter the velocity of each of its former moons relative to the Sun will remain and will be equal to sum of vectors of the velocity of Jupiter relative to the Sun and the velocity of the moons relative to Jupiter.

*Transcription note: the symbol $T$ labels the speed calculation in the source.*

A body can leave the Solar system if its total energy in the field of gravitation of the Sun would exceed zero:

$$-GMm/R+mv^2/2\ge0\quad\text{or}\quad mv^2/2\ge GMm/R.$$

But also we know that for a circular orbit

$$mv^2/2=GMm/2R.$$

Therefore, the body can leave the Solar system if its full speed at the distance of the orbit of Jupiter is at least $2^{1/2}$ times larger than the orbital velocity of Jupiter, i.e. $2^{1/2}\cdot13.07\,\mathrm{km/s}=18.48\,\mathrm{km/s}$. As we see, for any moon such a velocity is possible. At least, it is reached in a configuration of local opposition of the …

*[The continuation is cut off between the bottom of page 4 and the top of page 5. The next surviving word is reproduced below.]*

… disappears). The necessary drawing to this question should contain these sectors. Student have to find boundaries of the sectors geometrically from the diagram of geometrical summation of velocities or calculate the angles algebraically.

Answer: Io, Europa, Ganimede, Callisto, every moon in the case being in the sector shown at the drawing.

A body can fall into the Sun in the opposite situation, if the velocity relative to the Sun is strongly reduced, namely reduced to zero the orbital component of the velocity, then it will move to the Sun or from the Sun by a thin ellipse and finally fall into the Sun. Or, as an alternative we may keep the velocity large, but its vector should be directed strictly to the Sun, so that the point of perihelion of the (not closed) orbit appear in the Sun. By the same diagram of geometrical summation of velocities we may find that falling into the Sun is possible only for Io and Europa, and for both of them it will take place only in two points, sometime before the local conjunctions with Sun (analog to new moon at Earth) and sometimes after. The necessary drawing to this question should contain these points. The student has to find the points geometrically from the diagram of geometrical summation of velocities or calculate their positions algebraically.

Answer: Io and Europa in the case being in the points of orbit shown at the drawing.
